parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by the work function energy of a metal.

markscheme_points.text: minimum energy to remove electron or energy to remove electron from surface or energy to remove electron with zero kinetic energy

hints: Hint 1: Think about what a photon has to do to an electron in the metal - it must supply enough energy to free it from the attraction of the metal ions.
Hint 2: Focus on the word minimum - consider the easiest electron to remove, one at the surface that leaves with no spare kinetic energy.
parts.proper_answer: The minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of the metal, so that it leaves with zero kinetic energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture What Holds The Electron In**
Electrons in a metal are attracted to the positive ions. To get out into vacuum, an electron must be given energy to overcome this attraction. This is a one-photon to one-electron interaction.

Step 2: **Why Minimum And Surface Matter**
Electrons deeper inside lose extra energy in collisions on the way out. The smallest energy bill is for an electron right at the surface that just escapes and is left with $$E_{k} = 0$$. That minimum energy is defined as the work function energy $\Phi$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: Ultraviolet radiation of frequency $1.36 \times 10^{15} \text{Hz}$ is incident, in a vacuum, on a metal surface. The power of the radiation incident on the surface is $8.36 \text{mW}$. Photoelectrons are emitted with a maximum kinetic energy of $3.09 \times 10^{-19} \text{J}$.
parts.text: Determine the number of photons incident on the surface per unit time.
hints: Hint 1: Start by linking the total power falling on the surface to the energy carried by each individual photon - power is energy delivered per second.
Hint 2: Recall how the energy of a single photon depends on frequency, then rearrange to find how many such photons are needed each second to give the total power.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy Of One Photon**
Each photon carries energy set by its frequency: $$E = hf$$ With $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ and $f = 1.36 \times 10^{15} \text{ Hz}$: $$E = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 1.36 \times 10^{15} = 9.02 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

Step 2: **From Power To Photon Rate**
Power is total photon energy per second. If $N$ is number per second: $$P = N hf$$ $$N = \frac{P}{hf}$$ Convert $8.36 \text{ mW} = 8.36 \times 10^{-3} \text{ W}$: $$N = \frac{8.36 \times 10^{-3}}{9.02 \times 10^{-19}} = 9.27 \times 10^{15} \text{ s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the work function energy $\Phi$ of the metal.
hints: Hint 1: Think of energy conservation for the surface electron - the incoming photon energy is split between freeing the electron and giving it kinetic energy.
Hint 2: You already know the photon energy $hf$ from (b)(i) and you are given the maximum kinetic energy, so consider how to isolate the work function energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply Energy Conservation**
For the fastest electrons emitted from the surface there is no wasted energy, so all the photon energy goes into the work function plus kinetic energy: $$hf = \Phi + E_{max}$$

Step 2: **Calculate $\Phi$**
Rearrange before substituting: $$\Phi = hf - E_{max}$$ $$\Phi = (9.02 \times 10^{-19}) - (3.09 \times 10^{-19}) = 5.93 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The frequency of the radiation incident on the surface in (b) is increased while the power remains constant.

State and explain the effect of this change on:
parts.text: the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons

markscheme_points.text: greater photon energy (and same work function)
so maximum kinetic energy is increased

hints: Hint 1: Consider what happens to the energy of each photon when frequency is raised, while the metal itself is unchanged.
Hint 2: Use the energy balance $hf = \Phi + E_{max}$ to decide what must happen to $E_{max}$ if $hf$ grows and $\Phi$ stays fixed.
parts.proper_answer: Maximum kinetic energy increases because photon energy $hf$ increases while $\Phi$ is unchanged, so $E_{max} = hf - \Phi$ increases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **More Energy Per Photon**
Photon energy is directly proportional to frequency, $$E = hf$$. Raising $f$ means every photon brings more energy to the surface.

Step 2: **Same Cost To Escape, More Left Over**
The metal is the same so $\Phi$ is unchanged. From $$E_{max} = hf - \Phi$$ a larger $hf$ minus the same $\Phi$ leaves a larger maximum kinetic energy for the photoelectrons.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: the rate of emission of photoelectrons.

markscheme_points.text: (greater photon energy and same power so) lower number of photons (per unit time)
(each electron absorbs one photon) so lower rate of emission

hints: Hint 1: Remember total power is fixed but each photon now carries more energy - think about how many photons per second are needed to keep the same total power.
Hint 2: Link photons to electrons - one absorbed photon can release at most one photoelectron, so consider how photon rate controls electron rate.
parts.proper_answer: Rate of emission decreases because same power with larger $hf$ means fewer photons per second, and each photon releases one electron.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Fewer Photons For The Same Power**
Power is $$P = N hf$$ with $P$ constant. If $f$ increases, $hf$ increases, so $N$, the number of photons per second, must decrease to keep $P$ the same: $$N = \frac{P}{hf}$$

Step 2: **Fewer Photons Means Fewer Electrons**
In the photoelectric effect one photon is absorbed by one electron. With fewer photons arriving per second, fewer electrons can be released per second, so the rate of photoelectron emission falls.
